Greater lizardfish (Saurida tumbil) exhibits a life history strategy typical of many demersal tropical fishes, where growth is rapid and reproductive investment begins early relative to maximum size. Field surveys conducted across the Gulf of Thailand indicate that females attain a total length at puberty of 28.6 cm [Lp = 28.6 cm], a metric derived from examining gonadal development in captured individuals. This value represents approximately half the ultimate total length for females, which has been recorded at 60 cm [Li = 60 cm] in the same region based on a multi-year sampling program. The transition from a yolk-sac larva to the onset of exogenous feeding occurs within a week of eclosion, and subsequent juvenile growth is pronounced during the first monsoon season. Comparative studies suggest that the length at first maturity in Saurida tumbil is consistent with patterns observed in other synodontids, where reproductive activity commences well before asymptotic size is approached, thereby ensuring multiple spawning events across the lifespan. The large difference between length at puberty and the ultimate length underscores a growth trajectory that prioritizes early fecundity while still permitting considerable somatic expansion in later adulthood.

Neonatal body mass in this species is remarkably low, with newly emerged prolarvae weighing approximately 0.00038 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00038 grams] immediately following chorion rupture. This figure is extrapolated from the egg diameter of the congener Saurida undosquamis, which measures 0.9 mm, and reflects the typical volume of a pelagic teleost egg before yolk resorption begins. During the initial endotrophic phase, the lecithotrophic larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves, and the transition to active feeding upon completion of yolk-sac resorption occurs when the larva is still well under a milligram. In contrast to the minimal mass at emergence, adult females can reach an ultimate wet weight of 1900 grams [Wwi = 1900 grams], representing a staggering several-million-fold increase in biomass from the prolarval stage. The allometric relationship underpinning this growth, based on length-weight regressions developed from commercial catch data, indicates that weight accumulates disproportionately as individuals approach the upper bounds of their size distribution.

The annual reproductive output of Saurida tumbil is substantial, particularly given the elevated temperatures of its shallow coastal habitats. Under the prevalent thermal regime of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], females achieve a maximum reproductive rate that equates to roughly 196 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 196 eggs per day] when averaged across an extended spawning season. This value is derived from dividing the total seasonal fecundity of 71,364 eggs by a 365-day interval, assuming continuous spawning activity typical of tropical lizardfish populations. Gravid individuals collected during peak spawning months exhibit asynchronous oocyte development, suggesting that females release batches of pelagic eggs repeatedly rather than in a single synchronized event. The sustained high temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C] appears to accelerate vitellogenesis and shorten inter-spawning intervals, thereby maximizing the daily reproductive rate. Comparable evaluations for Saurida undosquamis in cooler waters report markedly lower fecundity, underscoring the role of thermal regime in shaping the species' life-history tactics.

Longevity records for Saurida tumbil indicate that individuals in the wild have a maximum lifespan estimated at 7 years [am = 7 years] when maintained at a mean annual water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This figure, derived from otolith increment analysis of the oldest sampled individuals from populations in the South China Sea, reflects a moderate lifespan for a medium-sized demersal predator. The relationship between temperature and senescence is apparent when comparing conspecifics from the cooler peripheries of the species' range, where lower metabolic rates appear to extend longevity slightly beyond this value. In the warmer core of its distribution, however, accelerated physiological processes compress the life cycle, with most reproductive output occurring during the first three to four years. The 7-year estimate (7 years) [am = 7 years] thus represents an upper bound under the prevailing thermal conditions, and field observations suggest that natural mortality rates climb steeply after age five, with very few individuals surviving to the maximum recorded age at a temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C].

The size at which female Saurida tumbil become reproductively active, 28.6 cm [Lp = 28.6 cm] in total length, corresponds to an age of approximately 1.5 years under the standard thermal conditions of 27.9 °C, a growth rate that aligns with the species' rapid juvenile phase. Upon reaching this length at puberty, individuals begin contributing to the population's reproductive output, which collectively can be substantial given the high fecundity rates observed. The ultimate size of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm] is seldom attained, as the combined pressures of fishing mortality and natural senescence limit the number of individuals surviving to asymptotic dimensions. A reproductive female at ultimate size can weigh up to 1900 grams [Wwi = up to 1900 grams], representing a peak body condition from which she allocates resources toward repeated spawning events. The interplay between early maturity, high fecundity, and moderate longevity yields a life history that is well tuned to the warm, productive environments Saurida tumbil inhabits.
